After all, when he makes employees' contribution, he is entitled to deduct it from the wages. Thus, by force of the application of the statutory provisions, the liability to contribute during the relevant period, namely, 11.7.85 to 31.3.88, arose. The Insurance Court as well as the High Court correctly upheld the demand for contribution, but it is rather strange to conclude that the demand could not be enforced against a closed business. If this finding were to be accepted, it would not promote the scheme and avoid the mischief; on the contrary, it would perpetrate the mischief. Any employer could easily avoid statutory liability and deny the beneficial piece of social security legislation to employees by closing down the business before recovery, which certainly is not the intendment of the Act. It is equally fallacious to conclude that because the employees had gone away there is no liability to contribute. The liability to contribute arose from the date of commencement of the establishment and is a continuing liability till closure. The very object of establishing a common fund under Section 26 for the benefit of all employees would be thwarted if such a construction is adopted. The proceeding for recovery is in respect of the dues of contribution which arose prior to the closure on 31.3.88. Therefore, it matters little when notice was issued calling upon the establishment to pay the contribution, as such notice is only a reminder to the employer to discharge his statutory obligation.
sections.judgement: The appeal was allowed. The appellant Corporation is entitled to proceed with the recovery proceedings in accordance with law.

sections.facts: In the respondent Company there were two rival Unions of workmen, namely, Karamchari Union and Shramik Sangh. The Karamchari Union espoused the demand of the workmen employed by the Company in its Kanpur unit for upward revision of dearness allowance following an award of the Industrial Tribunal Delhi, which linked the dearness allowance of Delhi unit workmen to the consumer price index for Delhi prepared by Labour Bureau, Simla, substantially increasing their dearness allowance. In an attempt to thwart the demand, the Company entered into a settlement with the Shramik Sangh regarding dearness allowance and approached the Labour Commissioner for registration. Failing to obtain registration, the Company unilaterally enforced a new scheme of dearness allowance linked to the all India average consumer price index prepared by Labour Bureau, Simla. The Karamchari Union rejected this formula and pressed its demand, leading to the dispute being referred for adjudication. The Tribunal directed that the workmen of the Kanpur unit be paid dearness allowance linked to the all India consumer price index (1960=100) for Kanpur Centre compiled by Labour Bureau, Simla, but allowed no change on the question of neutralisation.
sections.argument: Before the Tribunal, the Company contended: (1) that the settlement arrived at with the Shramik Sangh would be binding on the members of the Karamchari Union and the dispute did not require adjudication on merits; and (2) that the Company was desirous of linking dearness allowance to the all India average consumer price index for working class with base 1960=100, and the Tribunal should avoid accepting the demand of a few workmen. Additionally, regarding paying capacity, it was not contended by the Company that it could not bear the additional financial burden.
sections.analysis: The Tribunal committed a grave error in accepting the collusive settlement as the starting point of the revision. While uniformity may appear attractive, uniformity amongst dissimilar persons becomes counterproductive; constitutional aspirations like 'equal pay for equal work' apply to basic wages, but in dearness allowance, uniformity between metropolitan areas and smaller centres destroys the concept. Dearness allowance compensates for the erosion of real wages due to price rise, which varies from centre to centre, giving it a distinct local flavour. Therefore, dearness allowance must depend upon where the workman works, regardless of whether the employer has an all-India operation. The region-cum-industry principle must inform industrial adjudication, and introducing an all-India average consumer price index would treat unequals as equals, causing irreparable harm. Furthermore, where a dearness allowance scheme is linked to an index whose base year changes, a fresh linkage requires an appropriate conversion ratio, without which the scheme becomes unworkable, ineffective, and unjust. In this case, the conversion ratio of 4.83 is valid and correct, and the Tribunal erred in failing to adopt it.
sections.judgement: Partly allowing the appeal of the workmen, the Supreme Court held that the workmen of the Kanpur unit of the Company should be paid dearness allowance according to the all India consumer price index number for Kanpur (1960=100) compiled by Labour Bureau, Simla, after applying the conversion factor (linking factor) of 4.83. Their dearness allowance cannot be linked to the all India average consumer price index.

sections.facts: The third respondent was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh in the general election held in 1962. The appellant, a voter of the constituency, filed an election petition challenging the election of the third respondent on several grounds including corrupt practices. The petition was accompanied by the requisite number of copies which were true copies and each of them bore the signature of the petitioner. But there was no attestation at the foot of the copies that they were true copies. The third respondent raised various preliminary objections and the Election Tribunal rejected all of them. Thereupon he filed a writ petition in the High Court praying for the issue of a writ quashing the Tribunal's order. The High Court accepted the contention and issued a writ as prayed for. The present appeal was filed with special leave granted by this Court.
sections.statute: Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 80 and Section 81(3).
sections.argument: The main contention of the third respondent was that since the copies of the petition did not contain an attestation stating that the copies were true copies, there had been a violation of the mandatory provision of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
sections.analysis: If there is a total or complete non-compliance with the provisions of section 81(3), the election petition might not be 'an election petition presented in accordance with the provisions of the part' within s. 80 of the Act. By the expression 'copy' in section 81(3), it was meant not an exact copy but only one so true that nobody by any possibility misunderstands it not being the same as the original. In the present case, the signatures on the copies cannot be held to have been merely intended to be a copy of those on the original, since a signature in original was not needed on the copy and writing or copying out the name of the signatory would suffice. The absence of a writing in the copy indicating the signature in the original would not detract the copy from being a true copy. The facts and circumstances of the case show that there has been a substantial compliance with the requirement of section 81(3). The wider question whether section 81(3) or a part thereof is mandatory or directory is left open.
sections.judgement: The appeal is allowed.

sections.facts: The appellant company manufactured railway wagons in accordance with the specifications, terms and conditions contained in the agreements entered between the appellant and the Railway Board from time to time. The Railway Board without charging any price supplied wheel sets, axle boxes and various other finished components of wagons, which were termed as "free supply items," to the appellant, which were used in the manufacture of wagons and supplied the complete wagons to the Railway Board. The invoice value of the wagon charged by the appellant did not include the value of the "free supply items." The central excise authorities issued show cause to the appellant as to why the excise duty be not computed and charged on the value of the complete wagon, including that of the "free supply items". The appellant challenged the show cause notices by filing a Writ Petition before the High Court. Holding that the excise duty could only be charged on the invoice value under the contract, the Single Judge allowed the petition. The appeal filed by the Respondents against the judgment of the Single Judge was allowed by the Division Bench of the Court, against which the present appeal was made by the appellant company, raising the question whether the excise duty was to be charged on the invoice value of the wagon or on the value of the completed wagon including that of the "free supply items".
sections.statute: Sections 3 and 4 of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944.
sections.analysis: Section 3 of the Act provides for levy of the duty of excise. It is a levy on goods produced or manufactured in India. Section 4 of the Act lays down the measure by reference to which the duty of excise is to be assessed. The duty of excise is linked and chargeable with reference to the value of the excisable good and the value is further defined in express terms by the said section. In every case the fundamental criterion for computing the value of excisable article is the normal price at which the excisable article or an article of the like kind and quality is sold or is capable of being sold by the manufacturer. What comes down from the assembly line of the appellant's factory is a complete wagon and as such the appellant, being manufacturer of wagons, is liable to pay duty of excise on the value of a complete wagon. The "free supply items" like wheel sets etc. in the process of manufacturing become part of the complete wagon and lose their identity. It hardly matters how and in what manner the components of the wagon are procured by the manufacturer, so long as the appellant is manufacturing and producing the goods called "wagons" it is liable to pay duty of excise on the normal value of the wagon.
sections.judgement: Appeal dismissed.

sections.facts: On the death of the holder of an impartible estate who represented the first branch his widow K got into possession claiming that the estate was the separate property of her husband and also under a will. Disputes arose between her and the members of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th branches of the family and these were settled amicably. S who was the senior member of the 3rd branch obtained village D and one fourth of certain pannai lands as absolute owner and executed a release deed on 6th May, 1890, in these terms: 'Whatever rights over the said zamin properties and in all other above mentioned properties S might possess he gives up such rights absolutely in favour of the said K and her heirs enabling them to enjoy them with the power of alienation thereof by gift, sale, etc. The said S and his heirs shall have no claim at all to the properties shown as belonging to K'. KS who represented the 2nd branch and had instituted a suit against K compromised the suit on the 10th May, 1890, under a deed which provided inter alia: (i) that the zamindari shall be enjoyed by K till her lifetime and that KS and his heirs shall after the lifetime of K enjoy the zamindari except village D which was given to S; (ii) village B and one fourth of certain pannai lands shall be given to KS absolutely; (iii) all other pannai lands, buildings and movables which belonged to K's husband shall be enjoyed by K and her heirs absolutely. On the death of K the estate became vested in Z, the son of KS. On the death of Z without issue the second branch became extinct and disputes arose with regard to the ownership of the pannai lands and buildings, village B, and the zamindari between the widow of Z (who was the grand daughter of K) and the senior members of the 3rd and 4th branches.
sections.analysis: To establish that an impartible estate has ceased to be joint family property for purposes of succession it is necessary to prove an intention, express or implied, on the part of the junior members of the family to give up their chance of succeeding to the estate. In each case it is incumbent on the plaintiff to adduce satisfactory grounds for holding that the joint ownership of the defendant's branch in the estate was determined so that it became the separate property of the last holder's branch. The test to be applied is whether the facts show a clear intention to renounce or surrender any interest in the impartible estate or a relinquishment of the right of succession and an intention to impress upon the zamindari the character of separate property. The right to bring about a partition of an impartible estate cannot be inferred from the power of alienation that the holder thereof may possess. In the case of an impartible estate the power to divide it amongst the members does not exist, though the power in the holder to alienate it is there, and from the existence of the one power the other cannot be deduced, as it is destructive of the very nature and character of the estate and makes it partible property. A member of a joint family owning an impartible estate can on behalf of himself and his heirs renounce his right of succession but any such relinquishment must operate for the benefit of all the members and the surrender must be in favour of all the branches of the family as representing all its members. General words of release in a release deed do not mean release of rights other than those then put up, and have to be limited to the circumstances which were in the contemplation of the parties when it was executed.
sections.judgement: Held: (i) that as KS was competent to alienate the pannai lands and buildings in favour of K and vest her with absolute title, and S had also agreed to give them to her absolutely, K became the absolute owner of these lands and buildings and these ceased to be part of the joint estate and devolved on the grand daughters of K as her stridhana heirs; (ii) in view of the arrangement of 1890 it was not open to any of the parties to deny that the village B was separated from the zemindari and given to KS absolutely as his private property, which consequently devolved on Z as separate property and on his death on his widow; (iii) the arrangement made in 1890 did not evidence a partition amongst the members of the joint family or prove an intention on the part of the junior members of the family to renounce their expectancy of succession by survivorship on failure of the male lineal descendants in the branch of KS; (iv) that the recitals in the release deed executed by S had to be read in the light of the compromise in the suit of KS, and the proper inference from both documents read together was that S renounced only his right to succeed to the zemindari immediately as the seniormost member of the family and did not renounce his right or the right of his branch to succeed to the zemindari by survivorship if and when occasion arose; the senior member of the 3rd branch was therefore entitled to succeed to the zamindari in preference to the senior member of the 4th branch and the widow of Z. Vadrevu Ranganayakamma vs Vadrevu Bulli Ramaiya, Sivagnana Tevar vs Periasami and Thakurani Tara Kumari vs Chaturbhuj Narayan Singh distinguished. Sartaj Kuari's case, Konammal vs Annadana, Collector of Gorakhpur vs Ram Sunder Mal, Sri Raja Lakshmi Devi Garu vs Sri Raja Surya Narayana and Directors etc. of L.& S.W. Ry. Co. vs Richard Doddridge referred to. The judgment of the Madras High Court affirmed.

sections.facts: An Ambassador car was purchased by M/s. Karamchand Thapar & Bros. (Coal Sales) Ltd., Delhi in the year 1966 and was transferred to respondent No. 1 United Collieries Ltd., the owners in relation to the North Chirimiri Collieries, and it was, therefore, the owner of the said vehicle. On and from the appointed day, i.e., May 1, 1973, the right, title and interest of the owners in relation to the coal mines specified in the schedule stood transferred to and became vested in the Central Government free from all encumbrances under sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. Immediately after nationalisation, the Deputy Custodian General, Coal Mines Authority Limited, Nagpur addressed a letter dated May 9, 1973 to the Technical Advisor to the North Chirimiri Collieries using the said staff car to hand it over to the custodian. The Managing Director, Western Division, Coal Mines Authority, by an order dated August 9, 1973/1983, directed the respondents to hand over possession of the car failing which they would be liable to prosecution under the Act. Thereupon, respondent No. 1 and the Technical Advisor assailed this order by a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Nagpur Bench of the Bombay High Court. The High Court, purporting to rely on the decision in New Satgram Engineering Works & Anr. v. Union of India, held that whether the staff car should be treated as belonging to the owner of a mine as part of the mine itself raised disputed questions of fact relating to its user to be determined on evidence, discharged the rule, and left the parties to have their rights adjudicated in a civil suit. Feeling aggrieved, the Union of India preferred the appeal by special leave as the question involved affected a large number of cases.
sections.statute: Section 3(1), Section 2(h), Section 2(h)(xi), and Section 2(h)(xii) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973; Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
sections.argument: The car was not handed over on the plea that it was not used by the Technical Advisor exclusively for the North Chirimiri Collieries but used by him for looking after the multifarious activities of the Thapar Group of industries, which was a composite concern with businesses other than coal mining; therefore, although the car belonged to respondent No. 1, the owners of the North Chirimiri Collieries, it was not a staff car 'belonging to the mine'.
sections.analysis: Parliament, by an enlarged definition of 'mine' in section 2(h) of the Act, has indicated the nature of the properties that vest, and whether a particular asset is taken within the sweep of section 2(h) depends on whether it answers the description given therein. The staff car was undoubtedly a fixed asset of the North Chirimiri Collieries, and belonging to respondent No. 1, the owners in relation to the said mine, being the staff car of the Technical Advisor, was a 'fixed asset' belonging to the mine. 'Fixed assets' in general comprise those assets held for the purpose of conducting a business, in contradistinction to assets held for converting into cash, including real estate, buildings, machinery, etc. The staff car, therefore, fell within the definition of 'mine' under section 2(h)(xii) and vested in the Central Government under section 3(1). Merely because the Technical Advisor was putting the staff car to personal use or for multifarious activities of the Thapar Group of Industries would not alter the true legal position, since subsequent user for a different purpose was not really germane. There is a difference in language between section 2(h)(xi) ('if solely used') and section 2(h)(xii) ('belonging to the owner of a mine, wherever situated'). The observations in New Satgram Engineering Works regarding resolving disputes by a civil suit depending on the nature of user were made in the context of section 2(h)(xi). The present case is clearly covered by section 2(h)(xii) and not section 2(h)(xi); thus, New Satgram Engineering Works is distinguished.
sections.judgement: Appeal allowed.

sections.facts: The appellant, an Advocate, tenanted a building belonging to the respondent. The respondent sued the appellant for possession of the premises and by a compromise, the appellant agreed to vacate the premises by a certain date. A decree in terms thereof was passed. Then the Act came into being which by extension of its operation applied to Chandigarh with effect from 4-11-1972.
sections.argument: It was contended that: (i) had the decree been passed but a few days later, the Act would have admittedly interdicted the eviction because of Section 13 thereof; and had the decree been made and executed a day before the extension of the Act, the years of litigative procrastination of eviction might have been impossible. The salvation of the appellant is certain if he be a "tenant" within the meaning of the Act and his eviction is certain if the definition of tenant does not cover him in its amplitude; and (ii) that the effect of the compromise decree is that the tenancy of the appellant has been terminated.
sections.analysis: An advocate, under this Act, enjoys special protection. Rent control legislation in a country of terrible accommodation shortage is a beneficial measure whose construction must be liberal enough to fulfil the statutory purpose and not frustrate it. The benefit of interpretative doubt belongs to the potential evictee unless the language is plain and provides for eviction. That intendment must, by interpretation, be effectuated. The expression 'tenant' includes 'a tenant continuing in possession after the termination of the tenancy in his favour'. It thus includes, by express provision, a quondam tenant whose nexus with the property is continuance in possession. The fact that a decree or any other process extinguishes the tenancy under the general law of real property does not terminate the status of a tenant under the Act having regard to the carefully drawn inclusive clause. Subudhi's case related to a statute where the definition in section 2(5) expressly included "any person against whom a suit for ejectment is pending in a court of competent jurisdiction" and specially excluded "a person against whom a decree or order for eviction has been made by such a court." The text, reinforced by the context, especially of section 13, convincingly includes ex-tenants against whom decrees for eviction might have been passed, whether on compromise or otherwise. Nobody has a case that the appellant is not continuously in possession. The conclusion is inevitable that he remains a tenant and enjoys immunity under section 13(1) of the Act. The execution proceedings must therefore fail, because the statutory roadblock cannot be removed.
sections.judgement: Accepting the appeal. A conflict is best resolved by the parties as both sides in the present case have produced an enlightened settlement by an agreement to sell the property in dispute by the respondent to the appellant.

sections.facts: The plaintiffs brought a suit for partition, two of them claiming to be the reversioners of Chandrappa and the third a purchaser of the interest of the reversioners, defendants 4, 5 and 7. They were thus entitled to a 5/6th share of the properties while the 6th defendant was entitled as a reversioner of Chandrappa to the remaining 1/6th share. The property was in the possession of the three sons of Nagayya, the first three defendants, who denied these properties ever belonged to Chandrappa and also that the plaintiffs 1 and 2 or defendants 4 to 7 were his reversioners. The main defence was that even if the properties belonged to Chandrappa, the defendants' father Nagayya became entitled to these as Chandrappa's illatom son-in-law, on the basis that Chandrappa had brought Nagayya into his family under an arrangement that the latter would marry his wife's sister's daughter Mangamma and inherit the entire property after Chandrappa's death. The trial court dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order and decreed the suit.
sections.statute: Section 53A
sections.argument: On certificate, the only contention raised by the appellant in this Court was that even though specific performance had not been sought, the contract itself would have the effect of transferring interest in the property to Nagayya on Chandrappa's death.
sections.analysis: Held that after enactment of Section 53A, the only case in which the English doctrine of equity of part performance could be applied in India is where the requirements of Section 53A are satisfied. In the instant case, Section 53A has no application. It must be held therefore that considerations of equity cannot confer on Nagayya or his heirs any title in the lands which under the statute could be conferred only by a registered instrument. Challa Papi Reddi vs Challa Koti Reddi, (1872) 7 Mad. H C. R. 25; Bha'a Nahana vs Parbhu Hari, (1877) 2 I.L.R. Bom. 67; Asita, Mohan Ghosh Moulik vs Mohan Ghosh Moulik, (1016) 20 G.W.N. 901; Venkatayyamma Rao vs Appa Rao, (1916) L. R. 43 1. A. 138; Ariff vs Jadunath Majamdar, Cal. 1235, held inapplicable. Ariff vs Jadunath Majumdar, (1931) L. R. 58 I.A. 91, relied on.
sections.judgement: The appeal, therefore, must be dismissed.

sections.facts: Frank Anthony Public School is a recognised unaided minority school within the meaning of Sections 2(x) read with 2(e), 2(o), and 2(t) of the Delhi School Education Act. In the matter of emoluments and conditions of service, such as leave, teachers and employees of the school lag far behind those of Government schools, and several other conditions of service also compare unfavourably. But for Section 12, if Sections 8 to 11 were applicable, they would be at least as well off as their counterparts in Government schools. Sometime after the filing of the writ petition, on May 9, 1986, during the daily break between 10:00 A.M. and 10:40 A.M., the teaching staff (except one or two on duty) and Class IV staff took out a silent march without speeches, slogan shouting, violence, or disruption of studies, and classes resumed normally. Despite a warning notice issued by the principal on April 10, 1986, a similar silent march was taken out on April 10, 1986. Consequently, the management issued suspension orders against four staff members (Mrs. Malik, Mrs. Dhar, Mrs. Balman, and Mr. Bush). The petitioner association challenged these suspension orders and sought a stay of their operation in the writ petition.
sections.statute: Chapter IV of the Delhi School Education Act, comprising Sections 8 to 12, deals with the 'Terms and conditions of service of employees of recognised private schools.' Section 10(1) requires that the scales of pay and allowances, medical facilities, pension, gratuity, provident fund, and other prescribed benefits of employees of a recognised private school shall not be less than those of employees of corresponding status in schools run by the appropriate authority. Section 12 provides that 'Nothing contained in this Chapter shall apply to an unaided minority school.' Chapter V, comprising Sections 13 to 15, contains provisions applicable to unaided minority schools, including Section 13 enabling the Administrator to make regulations regarding minimum qualifications for recruitment. The effect of Section 12 is to make Sections 8, 9, 10, and 11 inapplicable to unaided minority schools regarding Administrator's service rules, prior approval of the Director for dismissal/removal/reduction in rank/termination, appeals against such orders, approvals for suspension, and parity of pay scales and allowances.
sections.argument: The petitioner association filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution seeking equalisation of pay scales and service conditions with those of Government school counterparts and a declaration that Section 12 of the Act is void and unconstitutional as offending Articles 14, 21, and 23 of the Constitution. In response to the Rule Nisi, the respondents contended that: (i) the classification made by Section 12 was perfectly valid; (ii) but for Section 12, Sections 8 to 11 would interfere with the right guaranteed by Article 30 of the Constitution to religious and linguistic minorities to administer educational institutions of their choice; (iii) the school was an institution of great repute whose excellence spoke for itself and did not necessitate regulation by any other authority; (iv) the scale of fees had to be kept low to remain within reach of ordinary people, which prevented payment of higher salaries and allowances; and (v) if Section 12 were struck down and the management compelled to pay Government-scale salaries, the school would have to be closed down.
sections.analysis: There is a general and broad consensus that the right guaranteed to religious and linguistic minorities by Article 30(1) of the Constitution is to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. The extent of this right is determined with reference to making the institutions effective vehicles of education, and regulatory measures designed towards this goal do not impinge upon Article 30(1) so long as they do not nullify the right of management in substantial measure. As established in In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957, conditions cannot be imposed that force the surrender of Article 30(1) rights, nor does the right depend on receipt of aid. The excellence of instruction directly depends on the quality and contentment of the teachers; thus, service conditions prescribing minimum qualifications, pay scales, allowances, and living standards to prevent oppression or exploitation are permissible regulations. Therefore, Section 10 is a permissible regulation aimed at excellence and does not detract from Article 30(1). Section 8(1) is innocuous. Section 8(2), which requires prior approval of the Director for dismissal, removal, reduction in rank, or termination, interferes with minority management rights and is objectionable. However, Section 8(3) provides a reasonable and limited right of appeal to an independent judicial Tribunal. Sections 8(4) and 8(5) provide a sound safeguard against abuse by requiring approval within 15 days while preserving the right to order immediate suspension for gross misconduct. Section 9 is innocuous since Section 14 applies similar provisions. Sections 8(1), 8(3), 8(4), 8(5), 9, and 11 do not encroach upon minority administration rights, as also demonstrated by Parliament applying Chapter IV to aided minority institutions without offending Article 30(1).
sections.judgement: The Supreme Court allowed the writ petition, holding that Section 12 of the Delhi School Education Act, which makes the provisions of Chapter IV inapplicable to unaided minority schools, is discriminatory and void not only because it makes Section 10 inapplicable, but also because it makes Sections 8(1), 8(3), 8(4), 8(5), 9, and 11 inapplicable to unaided minority institutions. Section 8(2), however, interferes with the right of minorities to administer educational institutions and is inapplicable to minority institutions.

sections.facts: The appellant, a share broker carrying on business in the City of Bombay and a member of the Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association, was employed by the respondent for effecting sales and purchases of shares on her behalf. The appellant effected purchases of 25 shares of Tata Deferred and 350 shares of Swadeshi Mills to square the outstanding sales of the same number of shares standing in her name and sent the relative contract notes therefor to her. The appellant referred the dispute for arbitration to the Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association in pursuance of an arbitration clause in the contract notes. The arbitrators made an award in favour of the appellant in the absence of the respondent who declined to take part in the proceedings. The respondent filed an application for setting aside the award. The Bombay High Court held that the contracts in question were not ready delivery contracts as defined in section 3(4) of the Bombay Securities Contracts Control Act VIII of 1925 and that they were accordingly void under section 6 of the Act and therefore the arbitration clause and the proceeding taken thereunder culminating in the award were also void.
sections.statute: Section 3(4) and Section 6 of the Bombay Securities Contracts Control Act VIII of 1925; Rule 167 of the Rules framed by the Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association, Bombay.
sections.argument: The respondent repudiated the contracts on the ground that the appellant had not been authorised to close the transactions on the date mentioned by him and asked him to square them at a later date, while the appellant maintained that the transactions had been closed in accordance with her instructions. The respondent refused to submit to arbitration of the association on the ground that the contract notes were void and therefore no arbitration proceedings could be taken thereunder.
sections.analysis: Apart from the question whether the contracts in question were for ready delivery or not, they were outside the purview of section 6 of Bombay Act VIII of 1925 because they were not contracts for sale and purchase of securities. The dispute between the parties was as to whether the appellant was acting within the scope of his authority when he purchased the shares. If he was acting within his authority, the respondent was liable to him. If those purchases were unauthorised, the appellant was liable to the respondent for damages. In either case the dispute was one which arose out of the contract of employment of the appellant by the respondent as a broker and not out of any contract of sale or purchase of securities. The relationship between the respondent and the appellant was that of principal and agent, and not that of seller and purchaser. The contract notes sent by brokers to their constituents are not themselves contracts for sale or purchase of securities within section 6 of the Bombay Act VIII of 1925 but only intimations by the broker to the constituent that such contracts had been entered into on his behalf. It is settled law that to constitute an arbitration agreement in writing it is not necessary that it should be signed by the parties, and that it is sufficient if the terms are reduced to writing and the agreement of the parties thereto is established. The Rules framed by the Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association, Bombay form a code complete in itself and any question arising with reference to those Rules must be determined on their construction and it would be a mistake to read into them the statutory provisions enacted in the Bombay Act VIII of 1925.
sections.judgement: Held, that the contracts fell outside the purview of section 6 of Bombay Act VIII of 1925, and therefore the contract notes cannot be held to be void under Rule 167.

sections.facts: On October 5, 1960, the appellant agreed to perform certain construction work for the respondent, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act with its principal place of business in Bombay, under the terms and conditions of a written tender. Clause 12 of the tender provided for arbitration in case of disputes, and Clause 13 provided that, notwithstanding the place where work was executed, the contract was deemed to have been entered into at Bombay and the courts in Bombay alone had jurisdiction to adjudicate thereon. When disputes arose, the appellant filed a petition in the Court at Varanasi under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act for filing the agreement and making a reference to arbitration. The trial court held that the entire cause of action arose at Varanasi and that parties could not by agreement confer jurisdiction on the Bombay courts. In revisional jurisdiction, the Allahabad High Court held that Bombay courts had jurisdiction under general law and that, under Clause 13, the petition could not be entertained at Varanasi, directing the petition to be returned for presentation to the proper court. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave.
sections.statute: Section 20 and Section 41 of the Arbitration Act, 1940; Section 20(a), Explanation II to Section 20, and Order 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; and the Indian Companies Act.
sections.argument: The respondent contended that in view of Clause 13 of the arbitration agreement, only the courts at Bombay had jurisdiction. Further, it was contended that Explanation II to Section 20(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure refers only to statutory or Government corporations and not to companies registered under the Indian Companies Act.
sections.analysis: By virtue of Section 41 of the Arbitration Act, the Code of Civil Procedure applies in its entirety to proceedings under the Arbitration Act, and the jurisdiction of courts to entertain proceedings for filing an award is governed by the Code. Under Section 20(a) read with Explanation II of the Code, the respondent company, having its principal place of business in Bombay, was liable to be sued at Bombay. While parties cannot by agreement confer jurisdiction on a court that does not possess it under the Code, where two or more courts have jurisdiction under the Code, an agreement to have disputes tried in one such court is neither contrary to public policy nor violative of Section 28 of the Contract Act. Furthermore, Order 29 of the Code deals with suits by or against a corporation, and there is nothing in the Code to support the contention that a corporation under Section 20 means only a statutory corporation and not a company registered under the Indian Companies Act.
sections.judgement: Since the courts at Bombay had jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure, the agreement between the parties that the courts in Bombay alone shall have jurisdiction to try the proceedings relating to arbitration was binding between them.

sections.facts: Appellant Company filed criminal complaints under Section 630(1)(b) of the Companies Act and Section 406 of the IPC against its employees (the first respondent of each appeal) as they did not vacate the company quarters after about six months even after retirement. The Judicial Magistrate, First Class dismissed the complaints on the ground that they were not filed within the period of limitation of six months from the date of retirement of the respondent employees. The High Court, holding that the offence under Section 630(1) was not a continuing offence, dismissed the Company's revision petitions.
sections.statute: Section 630 and Section 630(1)(b) of the Companies Act; Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code; Section 473 and Chapter XXXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
sections.analysis:
The beneficent provision contained in Section 630, no doubt penal, has been purposely enacted by the legislature with the object of providing a summary procedure for retrieving the property of the company: (a) where an officer or employee of a company wrongfully obtains possession of property of the company, or (b) where having been placed in possession of any such property during the course of his employment, wrongfully withholds possession of it after the termination of his employment. It is the duty of the court to place a broad and liberal construction on the provision in furtherance of the object and purpose of the legislation which would suppress the mischief and advance the remedy. 'Officer' or 'employee' in Section 630 of the Companies Act includes both present and past officers and employees.

The expression 'continuing offence' has not been defined in the Code. The question whether a particular offence is a 'continuing offence' or not must necessarily depend upon the language of the statute which creates that offence, the nature of the offence and the purpose intended to be achieved by constituting the particular act as an offence. The concept of continuing offence does not wipe out the original guilt, but it keeps the contravention alive day by day. Courts when confronted with provisions which lay down a rule of limitation governing prosecutions should give due weight and consideration to Section 473 of the Code, an overriding provision enabling cognizance after expiry of limitation if necessary in the interest of justice.

The offence under Section 630 is not such as can be said to have consummated once for all. Wrongful withholding, wrongfully obtaining possession, or wrongful application of the company's property cannot be said to be terminated by a single act or fact, but subsists for the period until the property is delivered up or refunded. It is an offence committed over a span of time where the last act controls the commencement of limitation; it consists of a continuous series of acts enduring after the period of consummation on refusal to deliver up the property. It is not an instantaneous offence and limitation begins with the cessation of the criminal act. The offence continues until the property is delivered up or refunded, for failure of which subsection (2) prescribes punishment. Thus, the offence under Section 630 is a continuing offence and limitation must be computed accordingly.
sections.judgement: Appeals of the Appellant Company allowed. The complaints could not be said to have been barred by limitation. (W.M.I. Cranes Ltd. vs G.G. Advani & Anr. overruled).

sections.facts: The appellant was appointed to the Indian Administrative Service (Karnataka Cadre) in 1957. On May 5, 1990, while holding the post of Additional Chief Secretary to the Government of Karnataka, he was appointed as Chief Secretary to the Karnataka Government until further orders. Originally, there was one post of Chief Secretary in Karnataka. An ex-cadre post of Additional Chief Secretary was created with a declaration under Rule 9(1) of the IAS (Pay) Rules that its status and responsibilities were equivalent to the cadre post of Chief Secretary; this post was subsequently encadred on January 30, 1987, carrying the same pay as the Chief Secretary. In 1989, the post of Secretary, High Power Committee, was created under the designation Chairman, Hyderabad, Karnataka Development Board, and was declared equivalent in status and responsibilities to the cadre post of Additional Chief Secretary under Rule 9 of the IAS (Pay) Rules, with all three posts carrying equal pay. On January 3, 1991, the Cabinet took a decision to effect a change of Chief Secretary. Pursuant thereto, on January 4, 1991, the Chief Minister took decisions and passed consequential orders: (i) declaring the post of Secretary, High Power Committee, equivalent in status and responsibilities to the post of Chief Secretary, (ii) transferring the appellant to that post with immediate effect, and (iii) appointing the 4th respondent, senior to the appellant, as Chief Secretary. The notification effecting the transfer was issued on January 4, 1991, but the authenticated Government order declaring equivalence under Rule 9 of the IAS (Pay) Rules was issued the next day, January 5, 1991. The appellant challenged the transfer order before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Bangalore, which dismissed the application holding that it was the prerogative of the Chief Minister and Cabinet to appoint a person of their confidence as Chief Secretary, that the appellant had no subsisting right to remain in the post, and that he failed to establish any ulterior motive. The appellant appealed by special leave.
sections.statute: Rule 9 and Rule 9(1) of the Indian Administrative Service (Pay) Rules, 1954.
sections.argument:
The appellant challenged the transfer order on two grounds: (1) that it was passed mala fide by the Chief Minister due to displeasure over the appellant's resistance to proposals regarding the posting of senior officers, rather than for administrative exigencies; and (2) that it was vitiated for non-compliance with procedural formalities since no declaration of equivalence under Rule 9(1) of the IAS (Pay) Rules, 1954 was in place when the transfer was made. The appellant further argued that prior declarations lost force upon the encadrement of the post of Additional Chief Secretary because equivalence pertains only to ex-cadre posts, and that simultaneous orders passed in undue haste showed a lack of bona fide exercise. 

The respondents denied the allegations of malice as scandalous and vexatious, contending that the post of Secretary, High Power Committee had already been declared equivalent to Additional Chief Secretary, which was interchangeable and equivalent to Chief Secretary. Before the Supreme Court, the Attorney General argued that respondent No. 4 was senior to the appellant and had no departmental proceedings pending against him, making the Cabinet's decision to appoint him as Chief Secretary neither perverse nor unjustified, but a legitimate exercise of prerogative.
sections.analysis:
The Supreme Court observed that the appellant failed to lay any firm foundation warranting a finding that the transfer order was passed mala fide or for an oblique purpose to punish or humiliate him. Pleadings merely showing that some of his suggestions on postings were not accepted by the Chief Minister did not establish mala fides. While it may not always be possible to demonstrate malice in fact with elaborate particulars and reasonable inferences may be drawn, such inferences must rest on a factual matrix and cannot remain in the realm of insinuation, surmise, or conjecture. The Chief Secretary and Chief Minister admittedly had differences of opinion on sensitive matters; relieving the appellant to post a senior officer of their confidence was not per se illegal or beyond administrative authority (relying on E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu).

Regarding the lack of declaration of equivalence under Rule 9(1) of the IAS (Pay) Rules, there had already been a declaration of equivalence between the post of Secretary, High Power Committee, and the post of Additional Chief Secretary, and the State Government maintained both posts were equivalent. Furthermore, the decision to declare the post equivalent to Chief Secretary had been taken prior to the impugned orders; the mere fact that formal publication could only be made the next day on January 5, 1991, did not invalidate the transfer order.
sections.judgement: The appeal was dismissed.

sections.facts: The respondent, in the first of these appeals, was manufacturing different varieties of printing paper including wrapping paper falling under Item No. 17 of the erstwhile Central Excise Tariff. The appellant issued a show cause notice to the respondent for the alleged violation of Rules 9(1), 173 F and 173 G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 in respect of wrapping paper removed outside the factory without payment of Central Excise duty, and for imposition of penalty. The Superintendent (Technical) held against the respondent, and on appeal, the Collector (Appeals) rejected the claim. On further appeal, the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal referred to its own decision, which is the subject matter of the other appeals herein, and set aside the order of the Collector. The facts leading to the other appeals are similar, and the issue involved is the same. The Revenue filed the appeals before the Supreme Court under Section 35L of the Central Excises & Salt Act.
sections.statute: Item No. 17 of the erstwhile Central Excise Tariff; Rules 9(1), 173 F, and 173 G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944; Section 2(f) and Section 35L of the Central Excises & Salt Act; and Notification No. 18A/83 CE dated 9th July, 1983.
sections.argument: Showing cause, the respondent contended that the wrapping paper was captively consumed and utilised as a component part of other varieties of paper and as such no duty was payable, placing reliance on Section 2(f) of the Act and Notification No. 18A/83 CE dated 9th July, 1983. On behalf of the Revenue, it was contended that wrapping paper cannot be deemed to be a component part because it did not become an integral part of the packed paper. The assessee contended that wrapping paper was a raw material or component part of the wrapped paper, relying on Section 2(f) of the Act which includes any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product. It was also urged that Revenue had itself considered the stage of wrapped or packed paper as the stage at which goods should be entered in the statutory production register.
sections.analysis: 'Manufacture' in the sense it is used in excise law is not complete until and unless wrapping is done. Excise is a duty on manufacture, which is the process or activity bringing into existence new, identifiable, and distinct goods that are marketed or marketable in the market as such. Duty is levied on goods, and as the Act does not define 'goods', the word carries its ordinary dictionary meaning as something that can ordinarily come to the market to be bought and sold and is known to the market as such. The finished goods were cut to size and packed paper which, according to trade practice and Indian standards, consisted of wrapping paper and wrapped paper; the market was for paper packed and wrapped in paper. Therefore, anything entering into and forming part of that process must be deemed to be raw material or a component part of the end product used in its manufacture. Processes incidental or ancillary to wrapping are included in manufacture, and manufacture is not complete until wrapped. Where any process is so integrally connected with ultimate production that, but for it, manufacture or processing would be commercially inexpedient, articles required in that process fall within 'in the manufacture of goods'. To be marketable, it was an essential requirement for goods to be wrapped in paper; anything required to make goods marketable forms part of manufacture, and materials used for the same constitute component parts for the end product.
sections.judgement: The appeals were dismissed.

sections.facts: On 15.3.1951, the appellant was appointed as a Pharmacist, which was then designated as compounder. On 13.2.1976, he was retired compulsorily by the Government under the first proviso to sub-rule (a) of Rule 71 of the Orissa Service Code. The appellant challenged the order by way of a writ petition in the High Court contending that the order was the result of ill will and malice the Chief District Medical Officer bore towards him, that his entire service was spotless, and that at no time were any adverse entries in his confidential character rolls communicated to him. The respondent Government submitted that the decision to retire the petitioner compulsorily was taken by the Review Committee and not by the Chief Medical Officer, and that besides remarks in confidential character rolls, other material was considered by the Review Committee bonafide and in the public interest. The High Court looked into the proceedings and character rolls and dismissed the writ petition, holding that an order of compulsory retirement after the prescribed qualifying service does not amount to punishment, was passed by the State Government, and uncommunicated adverse remarks can be relied upon on proper material. The present appeal by special leave was filed against the decision of the High Court on the question of whether acting upon undisclosed material was a ground for quashing the order of compulsory retirement. C.A. No. 870 of 1987 was also filed on similar facts.
sections.statute: First proviso to sub-rule (a) of Rule 71 of the Orissa Service Code; Fundamental Rule 56(j); Article 14 and Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
sections.argument: It was contended by the appellant that since an order of compulsory retirement had adverse effects upon the career and prospects of the government servant, the order should be passed in accordance with principles of natural justice; that before passing the order, a notice to show cause against the proposed order should be given to the government servant; that the order of compulsory retirement was based upon uncommunicated adverse remarks and that the appellant was also not afforded an opportunity to make a representation against the same; and that as per the new concept of Article 14 adumbrated in Maneka Gandhi case, any and every arbitrary action was open to judicial scrutiny.
sections.analysis: An order of compulsory retirement is not a punishment and implies no stigma nor any suggestion of misbehaviour. The order is passed on the subjective satisfaction of the government upon forming the opinion that it is in the public interest. The nature of the function is not quasi-judicial, and there is no room for importing any facet of natural justice. However, judicial scrutiny is not excluded altogether; courts may interfere under Article 226 if satisfied that the order is passed mala fide, is based on no evidence, or is arbitrary in the sense that no reasonable person would form the requisite opinion. An order of compulsory retirement is not liable to be quashed merely on the showing that uncommunicated adverse remarks were taken into consideration. Adverse remarks ought to be communicated in normal course and representations dealt with promptitude, but action under F.R. 56(j) or a corresponding rule need not await the disposal or final disposal of such representations, nor be held back merely because some adverse remarks of recent years are uncommunicated. The government or Review Committee must consider the entire service record, attaching more importance to the record and performance during later years; if promoted to a higher post notwithstanding adverse remarks, such remarks lose their sting, especially when promotion is based upon selection.
sections.judgement: The appeals were dismissed.

sections.facts: The Governor of U.P. issued a Notification under Section 3 A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, and the Sales Tax Officer (Section IV) Kanpur ordered the respondent company to pay tax on the turnover of carbon paper at 6%, and that of ribbon at 10%, as per entry 2 of the Notification. The respondent challenged the order in a writ petition before the High Court, and the High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the levy.
sections.statute: Section 3 A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948.
sections.argument: The respondent contended that carbon paper was not 'paper' within the meaning of entry 2 and its turnover was therefore to be assessed at the rate of 2% prescribed for unclassified goods, and that 'ribbon' being an accessory and not a part of the typewriter could only be taxed at the rate of 6% and not 10%. The appellant contended that carbon paper does not lose its character as paper in spite of being subjected to chemical processes, and that ribbon is not an accessory but an essential part of the typewriter.
sections.analysis: A word which is not defined in an enactment has to be understood in its popular and commercial sense with reference to the context in which it occurs, and according to the well-established canon of construction, in the sense in which persons dealing in and using the article understand it. The word 'paper' is understood as meaning a substance used for bearing writing or printing, for packing, for drawing on, or for decorating or covering walls. Carbon paper cannot be used for these purposes but is used for making replicas or carbon copies, and cannot properly be described as paper. This rule of construction equally applies to ribbon, which is an accessory and not a part of the typewriter, though it may not be possible to type out any matter without it.
sections.judgement: Appeal dismissed.

sections.facts: The appellants filed a suit in the court of a subordinate judge. At the instance of respondent No. 1 (who was the defendant in the suit) an issue as to the jurisdiction of the court to try the suit was framed. Holding that it had no jurisdiction to try the suit, the civil court returned the plaint to the appellants for presentation to the proper revenue court. The revenue court, on presentation of a petition by the appellants, held that it had no jurisdiction to try it. Thereupon the appellants again filed a suit in the court of the subordinate judge. The suit failed on the ground of res judicata. On appeal, the High Court upheld the view of the civil court.
sections.argument: The question arose as to whether the decision of the subordinate judge on the preliminary issue operated as res judicata.
sections.analysis: If in a case, the defendant does not appear and the Court, on its own, returns the plaint on the ground of lack of jurisdiction, the order in a subsequent suit may not operate as res judicata; but if the defendant appears and an issue is raised and decided, then the decision on the question of jurisdiction will operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit, although the reasons for its decision may not be so. In the instant case, in the first suit the appellants ought to have insisted that the suit was triable by the civil court, or they should have taken the matter before a higher Court in the revenue proceeding. The appellants did neither. The revenue court had no jurisdiction to go behind the decision of the civil court. Upendra Nath Bose vs Lall & Ors., AIR 1940 P.C. 222 held inapplicable; Jwala Debi vs Amir Singh, AIR 1929 All. 132 not approved.
sections.judgement: Appeal dismissed.

sections.facts: An inspector of the Delhi Electric Supply Undertaking demanded a bribe for giving the complainant a power connection for his factory. Information having been given to the anti-corruption police, a trap was set. The inspector did not turn up at the appointed time to receive the money, but the appellant, a permanent labourer working under him, came to the complainant's factory, told him that he had been sent by the inspector, and that the money should be given to him. The complainant, at first, insisted that the inspector himself should come but later gave him the money. The money was recovered from the appellant, and the inspector and the appellant were charged with offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act. The trial court acquitted the inspector but convicted the appellant under Section 5(2) read with Section 5(1)(d) of the Act, and under Section 161 I.P.C., with the aid of the presumption under Section 4(1) of the Act. The conviction was confirmed by the High Court.
sections.statute: Section 4(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act provides that in the trial of an offence punishable under Section 161 or 165, I.P.C., or under clauses (a) or (b) of Section 5(1) read with sub-section 5(2) of the Act, if the prosecution proves that the accused had accepted or obtained a gratification other than legal remuneration, the court has to presume that the gratification was accepted or obtained by the accused as a motive or reward as mentioned in Section 161, I.P.C.
sections.analysis:
The question whether a government servant receiving money had the requisite incriminatory motive is one of fact. One of the essential ingredients of the offence under Section 161, I.P.C., is that the gratification must have been received by the accused as a motive or reward for committing an act or omission in connection with his official functions. Even if the government servant was incapable of showing any favour or rendering any service in connection with his official duties, he may be guilty; but the existence of an understanding that the bribe was given in consideration of some official act or conduct is an important factor bearing on whether the accused received the gratification as a motive or reward as mentioned in Section 161, I.P.C.

The appellant, being a mere labourer, was incapable of showing any favour or rendering any service to the complainant in connection with his official duties. It had not been shown by the prosecution that he was in any way officially concerned with the installation of poles or the giving of the electric connection; nor was it shown that the appellant made any representation, claim or promise that he would, either himself or through his inspector, get an official act done for the complainant, or that he had demanded a bribe from the complainant. In the absence of any such circumstances, the conduct of the appellant was not incompatible with the role of an innocent carrier of money without the requisite mens rea. The charge under Section 5(1)(d) also is unsustainable because it could not be reasonably said that the appellant obtained the money by using corrupt or illegal means or otherwise abusing his official position as a public servant.

The presumption under Section 4(1) of the Act is not absolute and is rebuttable. The quantum and nature of proof required to displace the presumption varies according to the circumstances of each case, and may partake of the shape of defence evidence adduced by the accused or consist of circumstances appearing in the prosecution evidence itself as a result of cross-examination or otherwise. While the mere explanation given by the accused in his examination under Section 342, Cr.P.C., may not be enough, the burden on him to negate the presumption may stand discharged if the effect of the material brought on record, in its totality, renders the existence of the fact to be presumed improbable. The accused may rebut the presumption by showing a mere preponderance of probability in his favour, and it is not necessary to establish his case beyond reasonable doubt. Further, the sole purpose of the presumption under Section 4(1) is to relieve the prosecution of the burden of proving a fact which is an essential ingredient of the offence under Section 5(1) and (2) of the Act and Section 161, I.P.C.; it can be used only in furtherance of the prosecution case and not in derogation of it. In the present case, the statutory presumption being antithetical to the prosecution story—namely, that it was the inspector who demanded the bribe for showing a favour and that the payment was intended for him—could not be availed of by the prosecution against the appellant.

Nor can the appellant be held guilty of abetting the alleged attempt made by the inspector to obtain illegal gratification. Intention to aid the commission of the crime is the gist of the offence of abetment, and such intention on the part of the appellant is lacking, as it was not shown that he was present on any occasion when the inspector demanded the bribe. Moreover, the principal accused had been acquitted. The prosecution having failed to prove that the money had been paid to the appellant pursuant to the demand for a bribe by the inspector, the court cannot make out a new case for the prosecution and hold that the amount had been received by the appellant on his own or for some person other than the inspector.
sections.judgement: Appeal to this Court allowed.

sections.facts: In the instant case the charge against the appellant workman was that he had used threatening and abusive language against a senior officer unbecoming of a disciplined workman and had adopted a threatening posture, subversive of discipline. An inquiry was conducted, and on the recommendations of the Inquiry officer, the workman was dismissed from service. The Labour Court upheld the order of dismissal and the High Court dismissed the appellant's petition under Article 227. The appellant workman had put in more than 14 years of service and had been the Secretary of the workers' union, and the management had not shown that there was any blameworthy conduct on his part during the period of his service.
sections.statute: Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act and Article 136 and Article 227 of the Constitution of India. Under Section 11A, the Labour Court is clothed with jurisdiction and power to substitute its measure of punishment in place of managerial wisdom once it is satisfied that the order of discharge or dismissal was not justified in the facts and circumstances of the case. The words that the court must be 'satisfied that the order of discharge or dismissal was not justified' indicate that even though misconduct is proved, the extreme penalty was either disproportionately heavy or excessive. Under Article 136, the Court can examine whether the Labour Court properly approached the matter in exercising or refusing to exercise its power under Section 11A.
sections.analysis: In order to avoid the charge of vindictiveness, justice, equity and fairplay demand that punishment must always be commensurate with the gravity of the offence charged. In the development of industrial relation norms, law has moved far from the days when quantum of punishment was considered a managerial function with courts powerless and incapable of curing injustice where punishment was disproportionately heavy. It is a well-recognized principle of jurisprudence permitting penalty for misconduct that it must be commensurate with the gravity of the offence charged. The misconduct alleged consisted of the use of language which was indiscreet and improper, disclosing a threatening posture, which is the subjective conclusion of the hearer because voice modulation differs. While indiscreet, improper, abusive language may show lack of culture, the mere use of such language on one occasion unconnected with any subsequent positive action and not preceded by any blameworthy conduct cannot permit an extreme penalty of dismissal from service.
sections.judgement: The order of dismissal was not justified.

sections.facts: The appellant was the auction purchaser of the property at a revenue sale held under the provisions of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, for recovery of land revenue due. At the time of the attachment and sale, the property was in the possession of a Receiver appointed under Order 40, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the Bombay High Court. Notice of the attachment and sale was not given to the Receiver, nor was any leave of the Court taken for the sale. The Receiver instituted a suit for a declaration that the sale was a nullity or, at any rate, was illegal and liable to be set aside.
sections.statute: Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, Sections 156, 157, and 192(1); Code of Civil Procedure, Order 40, Rule 1.
sections.argument: The auction purchaser contended that the sale without notice to the Receiver or without impleading him was not void but only voidable, and that, in any event, the suit was barred by the provisions of Sections 157 and 192 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928.
sections.analysis: Sub-section (1) of Section 157 of the Code, which bars the institution of a suit to set aside a sale, is confined only to claims on the ground of irregularity or mistake in publishing or conducting the sale as referred to in Section 156; suits based on other grounds, including those referred to in sub-section (2) of Section 157, are not within the prohibition of sub-section (1). Section 192 of the Code is not applicable as the suit is not one simpliciter to set aside the sale held by the revenue authorities, but one for a declaration and consequential relief on grounds taken by the Receiver that are not covered by the specific provisions of the Code for setting aside a sale which the revenue authorities are empowered to determine, decide, or dispose of within the meaning of Section 192(1).
sections.judgement: Held, (1) that the sale was illegal in the absence of the leave of the Court and the necessary notice to the Receiver; and (2) that the suit was not barred by any of the provisions of the Code.

sections.facts: By clause 4 of a will, the testator bequeathed to his granddaughters T and S an absolute right in the properties that were to devolve on them after the death of his wife. Clause 5 further provided that if one of the two granddaughters were to die issueless, the other living granddaughter was to enter into possession of the entire property as absolute owner. After the death of the testator's wife, T and S divided the properties which devolved on them in equal shares. On S dying issueless, T instituted a suit for possession of the properties that fell to the share of S, basing her claim on clause 5 of the will. The suit was dismissed.
sections.analysis: Clause 5 of the will relates to devolution; it does not provide for any divestment of an estate which had vested. The estate that vested in S under clause 4 of the will was not a conditional estate, but an absolute one, and the will does not provide for the divestment of that estate. Clause 5 would have come into operation if the contingency mentioned therein had happened before the properties absolutely devolved on T and S. What the testator intended was that if any of his granddaughters died issueless before the devolution took place, then the entire property should go to the other granddaughter; this intention is plain from the language of the will. Section 124 applies to the facts of the case and not section 131. The legacy claimed by the appellant is unavailable as the contemplated contingency did not occur before the fund bequeathed was payable or distributable. Section 131 provides for the divestment of an estate which had already vested and speaks of an estate going over to another person. (Norendra Nath Sircar and anr. vs Kamal Basini Dasi, referred to).
sections.judgement: Dismissing the appeal.

sections.facts: The City Corporation of Bangalore invited objections from the public to the proposed levy of octroi on certain items. In a meeting of the Corporation, after placing the objections on the Table and circulating the Notes of the Commissioner analysing the objections, a unanimous resolution was passed levying the octroi. The High Court declared the Resolution invalid holding that because of shortage of time, the condition precedent for passing the resolution, i.e., real consideration of the objections, was not satisfied. Hence, these appeals were filed by the Corporation.
sections.statute: Section 98(1) of the City of Bangalore Corporation Act, 1949.
sections.argument: The respondents challenged the validity of the Resolution contending that it was passed in violation of Section 98(1) of the City of Bangalore Corporation Act, 1949.
sections.analysis:
Taxation in order to be valid must not only be authorised by a statute, but also be levied or collected in strict conformity with the statute which authorises it. Where a condition precedent is laid down for statutory power being exercised, it must be fulfilled before a subordinate authority can exercise delegated power. When the statute requires that delegated power may be exercised on fulfilment of certain conditions precedent, the Court would presume the regularity of the order including the fulfilment of the condition precedent. It is for the party who challenged the legality to show that the condition precedent was not in fact complied with by the authority.

The Municipal Administration is coordinated to secure the vital interest of the general public. It is the function of the representative body to ascertain the local opinion and decide thereon before imposition of the tax. It has, therefore, to be assumed that local representatives who had taken note of the objections received in pursuance of the notice published have consciously reached the decision. Once it is clear that there had been consideration of the objection, it is not for the Court to examine the manner in which the legislative will had been indicated.

The Court has no jurisdiction to examine the validity of the reasons that go into the decision or the motive that induced the delegated authority to exercise its powers. No judicial duty is laid on the authority in discharge of the statutory obligations, and, therefore, the only question to be examined is whether the statutory provisions have been complied with.

The High Court was not justified in assuming from the time factor alone that there could not have been a consideration of the objections. It is not the function of the Court to probe into the details of the discussions and deliberations before legislative will is expressed by passing the resolution. The connotation of the word 'consideration' occurring in sub-section (1) of Section 98 comprehends 'taking note of' or 'paying heed to' depending upon the nature of the subject. It may be open to the councillors to express their views even within the limited time available; no standard can be prescribed in such matters. When it is shown that the council had the opportunity to consider the objections received, it has to be deemed that they had taken note of the same before reaching a decision.
sections.judgement: The judgment of the High Court was set aside and the appeals were allowed.

sections.facts: The writ petition was originally filed by two members of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service, Shri R.L. Gupta and Shri S.B. Aggarwal, but was subsequently confined to Shri R.L. Gupta. The petitioner, confirmed as a Sub-Judge in the Delhi Judicial Service in August 1971, was working as an Additional District and Sessions Judge when, on May 14, 1981, he was sent on deputation as Member Secretary of the Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board. On April 26, 1985, the Government of India appointed a Commission of Inquiry presided over by Shri Justice Ranganath Misra to inquire into incidents of violence following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Upon the Central Government's request and the petitioner's consent, the High Court permitted him to go on deputation as Secretary to the Commission with effect from June 1, 1985, at his own risk. Within three months, the Chief Justice of the Delhi High Court requested Justice Misra to relieve the petitioner within ten days as his turn to be placed on probation had arrived. Justice Misra responded that it was difficult to relieve him in the public interest. Consequently, on November 22, 1985, the High Court passed a resolution treating the petitioner as having refused to return at his own risk, rejected his case for probation, and placed seventeen junior judicial officers (commencing with Shri Jaspal Singh and four others) on probation ahead of him. After the Commission completed its work, the petitioner was reposted as Additional District and Sessions Judge and placed on probation from April 4, 1987. Aggrieved by this supersession, the petitioner approached the Court.
sections.statute: Rule 16 of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules; Rule 4 read with the Schedule attached to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1970.
sections.argument: It was submitted on behalf of the High Court that the petitioner, having been informed that he was proceeding on deputation at his own risk, could not retain his seniority over his juniors who were placed on probation during that period. The Additional Solicitor General of India appearing on behalf of the Union of India supported the petitioner's case.
sections.analysis: No specific rules governing the deputation of an officer working in the judicial department were produced, requiring the matter to be determined on principles of justice, equity, and judicial precedents. Undisputedly, the petitioner would have been placed on probation on November 22, 1985, as a matter of course had he remained in his parent cadre. Officers are routinely sent on deputation in the public interest with their consent, and merely giving consent cannot cause them to suffer adverse consequences in the absence of a specific rule or good reason, in line with State of Mysore v. M.H. Bellary and State of Mysore v. P.N. Nanjundiah. The petitioner was on temporary deputation under a Supreme Court Judge and could not leave without permission; moreover, the Chairman issued a high commendation of his efficiency and legal acumen. The object of probation is to assess suitability, which can equally be made by the authority under whom the officer works on deputation. It was not a true case of refusal to return by the petitioner, nor could the Chairman's refusal to relieve him be held against him. Furthermore, keeping cadre strength artificially low and placing promotees on probation nearly nine years after promotion is a farce. The Court also observed that the Delhi Administration should increase judicial posts and address appallingly high court arrears on a war footing without treating finance as a constraint.
sections.judgement: The writ petition was allowed. The Court held that the petitioner should have been placed on probation on November 22, 1985, notwithstanding his deputation. The Court directed that the petitioner be deemed to have been on probation from November 22, 1985, that his services be regulated accordingly, and that he be deemed placed above Shri Jaspal Singh in the seniority list of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. Other contentions were left open.

sections.analysis: It may be taken as well settled that there is no warrant for the proposition of law that when a grant of immoveable property is made to a Hindu female she does not get an absolute or alienable interest in such property unless such power is expressly conferred upon her. The law is that there is no presumption one way or the other and there is no difference between the case of a male and the case of a female and the fact that the donee is a woman does not make the gift any the less absolute where the words would be sufficient to convey an absolute estate to a male. Mohamed Shumsool vs Shewakram (2 I.A. 7), Nagammal vs Subbalakshmi 1(1947) I.M.L.J. 641 and Ram Gopal vs Nand Lal (A.I.R. referred to.

sections.facts: Under a scheme for taking over certain stage carriage services to the complete exclusion of private operators, which was approved and notified by the State of Mysore under Chapter IV A of the Motor Vehicles Act, it was provided, inter alia: "The State Transport Undertaking will operate services to the complete exclusion of other persons (i) on all the notified inter district routes except in regard to the portions of inter district routes Lying outside the limits of Mysore District, and also (ii) over the entire length of each of the inter district routes Lying within the limits of Mysore District." The appellants were running stage carriage omnibuses on certain routes, some of which were inter district and inter State.
sections.statute: Chapter IV A of the Motor Vehicles Act.
sections.argument: The appellants challenged the validity of the scheme on the ground, inter alia, that between the routes which were taken over and some of the inter district and inter State routes which were left to the private operators, there was an overlap in the Mysore District, and that those routes which were not taken over, including the portion of the route lying within the Mysore District, should not be affected by the scheme, because "route" meant a notional line running between two termini and following a distinct course.
sections.analysis: The scheme of the Act is that the word "route" means not only the notional line but also the actual road over which the omnibuses run. Under the Act, the route or area stands for the road on which the omnibuses run or portions thereof. (Kondala Rao v. Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation relied on; Kelani Valley Motor Transit Co., Ltd. v. Colombo Ratnapura Omnibus Co., Ltd. explained and distinguished).
sections.judgement: In the present case, in view of the fact that the scheme reserved all the routes within the Mysore District to the State Transport Undertaking, the private operators would not be able to ply their omnibuses on that sector, and even those routes which were inter district open to them would stand pro tanto cut down to only that portion which lay outside the Mysore District. (Nilkanth Prasad v. The State of Bihar followed).

sections.facts: Sangita was married to accused 2 on 28th April, 1984. In the intervening night of 14/15 September 1984, the accused found Sangita burning.
