The landlord can recover possession of the property only on one or more of the grounds enacted in the relevant section of the Rent Acts. Even after the termination of the contractual tenancy the landlord under the definitions of the terms landlord and tenant contained in the Rent Acts, remains a landlord and the tenant remains a tenant, because of the express provision made in the enactments that a tenant means or includes 'a person continuing in possession after the termination of the tenancy in his favour'. Yet another important feature of the Rent Acts is that either by way of a non obstante clause or by necessary implication these enactments have done away with the law contained in section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act dealing with rights and liabilities of the lessor and the lessee. Maharaja of Jaypore vs Rukmani Pattamahdevi, 46 I.A. 109; A.I.R. [1919] P.C. 1 and V. Dhanapal Chattiar vs Yesodai Ammal, referred to. Sada Ram and Others vs Gajjan Shiama, A.I.R. 1970 Punjab & Haryana 511; Shiv Parshad vs Smt. Shila Rani, A.I.R. 1974 H.P. 22 and Machavaram Venkate Narayana Rao vs Sarvepalli Narayane Rao Sarada and another, relied upon.
sections.judgement: Dismissing the appeal by special leave.

sections.facts: The respondent let out his premises to the appellant by way of an unregistered lease deed which inter alia stated that without the permission of the landlord the premises should not be sublet except to associate concerns, and the lessee was liable for payment of rent. Alleging that the appellant, an automobile manufacturing company, had sublet the premises to M/s United Automobiles without his consent, the respondent initiated eviction proceedings. Both the Rent Controller and the appellate authority held that the term of the lease was not inadmissible, but ordered eviction on the ground that M/s United Automobiles was inducted in the premises as a sub-lessee. The appellant filed a second appeal before the High Court, which dismissed it in limine, leading to the present appeal by special leave.
sections.statute: Section 14(1) Proviso (b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act.
sections.argument: The appellant contended that M/s United Automobiles, being the authorised dealer and distributor of products manufactured by it, was in occupation of the premises in that capacity and could not be described as a sub-tenant. Alternatively, it contended that in view of the specific term in the lease deed, the arrangement with an associate concern was not a sublease without the landlord's consent. The respondent took the stand that the term could not be looked into as the document was not registered, and that M/s United Automobiles could not be assumed to be an 'associate concern' within the meaning of the term.
sections.analysis: The appellant created a sublease in favour of its dealer and parted with possession within the meaning of section 14(1) Proviso (b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act. The appellant company has a separate legal entity and has nothing to do with M/s United Automobiles except that the latter is the dealer-distributor of some of its manufactured articles. M/s United Automobiles is not a licensee and is not in possession of the premises on behalf of the appellant. Its monetary benefit is confined to commission received on vehicle sales and does not include the right of enjoyment of the premises, and the fixed rent it pays is independent of sales. Whether a lessee is entitled to sublease is a term of the lease transaction; if the document is inadmissible for non-registration, all its terms, including permission to sublease, are inadmissible. Furthermore, the clause contained consent only in general terms without reference to M/s United Automobiles, which was inducted much later. Such general permission cannot be treated as the consent required under section 14(1) Proviso (b) of the Act, which requires specific written consent.
sections.judgement: Appeal dismissed.

sections.facts: A trust with the settler, her son, and two others as trustees was created, with part of the trust property including a large house. The respondents in Criminal Appeal No. 658 of 1986 were employed as Secretary and Manager of the trust between 1976 and June 1981. On a complaint filed in the court of the Metropolitan Magistrate by one of the trustees alleging that these two officers, in conspiracy with the settler's son and his wife, created documents showing tenancy in respect of a flat in the house in favour of the trustee's wife, summons were issued against the four accused. The High Court quashed the proceedings against two accused but sustained the order against the other two accused. Appeals were filed in the Supreme Court by both the accused whose prosecution was not quashed and the complainant.
sections.statute: Sections 406 and 467 read with sections 34 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC); Section 53.
sections.argument: On behalf of the accused appellants, it was contended that the trust deed authorised the trustee to look after the affairs of the trust, and the tenancy in favour of his wife could not be considered as creating an interest in favour of the trustee since she was an independent person with her own income. It was argued that there was no mens rea, at most it amounted to a civil wrong, and the court machinery should not be utilised for private vengeance because the mother and son had fallen out. On behalf of the complainant, it was urged that under section 53, it was a clear case of breach of trust, which simultaneously constitutes a civil wrong and a criminal offence, and the complainant should be given an opportunity to lead evidence rather than entertain objections at a preliminary stage.
sections.analysis: When a prosecution at the initial stage is asked to be quashed, the test to be applied is whether the uncontroverted allegations prima facie establish the offence. The court must consider any special features to evaluate whether it is expedient and in the interest of justice to permit a prosecution to continue, as the court cannot be utilised for an oblique purpose. Where the chances of ultimate conviction are bleak and no useful purpose is served by continuing prosecution, the court may quash the proceedings at a preliminary stage. While a breach of trust may be both a civil wrong and a criminal offence, some situations are predominantly civil wrongs; here, the facts may at most constitute a civil wrong and the ingredients of a criminal offence are wanting. Considering the relevant documents, the trust deed, the correspondence, the family fallout, and the fact that the trustee's wife claims no interest in the tenancy, the criminal case should not be continued.
sections.judgement: The appeal of the accused is allowed, the appeal of the complainant is dismissed, and the criminal proceedings against the appellant-accused are quashed.

sections.facts: The appellant and its workmen, represented by their union called the Indoxco Labour Union, Jamshedpur, made a joint application to the Government referring certain disputes to the Industrial Tribunal. The application stated that the number of workmen employed in the undertaking affected were those employed in the company's factory at Jamshedpur, and that the same number were likely to be affected by the disputes. The Government referred the disputes to the Industrial Tribunal, and the notification also stated that the disputes were between the management of the appellant company's factory at Jamshedpur and their workmen represented by Indoxco Labour Union. Two of the demands were (1) payment of overtime to office staff should be 1 1/2 times the ordinary rate, and (2) the union representatives should be allowed special leave to attend law courts for matters connected with the workers and the management, to attend the annual conventions of their federation, to attend to Executive Committee meetings of the union federation and the conventions of the central organisation i.e., INTUC. The union at a general meeting, held prior to the reference, had passed a resolution changing the name of the union to Indian Oxygen Workers Union and making the workmen of all the establishments of the appellant company in Bihar eligible for its membership, informing the appellant company at Jamshedpur of this amendment by letter. The Tribunal held that: (i) the award was to apply to all of the workmen and could not be restricted to the workmen working at Jamshedpur; (ii) overtime work exceeding 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours per week should be paid at overtime rates, and if exceeding 48 hours per week, at double the ordinary rate of wages; and (iii) while rejecting the demand for special leave with pay to attend law courts as the company's existing concession was sufficient, the union's representatives were to be given special leave to attend meetings of its executive committee, meetings of the federation of the union, the annual convention of that federation when held at Jamshedpur, and the convention of the INTUC. The company appealed to the Supreme Court.
sections.statute: Sections 6(g), 28(3), 29 and 30(3) of the Trade Unions Act; Regulation 9 of the Central Trade Union Regulations; Bihar Shops and Establishments Act.
sections.argument: The company contended that under the provisions of the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, it could not be called upon to pay for overtime work anything more than its ordinary rate of wages if the workmen worked beyond 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours a week. In response to whether union meetings could be held outside work hours, it was argued that it may not always be possible to do so if an emergency arises.
sections.analysis: The agreement to refer the disputes for adjudication was between the management of the appellant company's factory at Jamshedpur and the workmen employed in that factory represented by Indoxco Labour Union. Even assuming the union validly amended its constitution to extend membership to other establishments, the award must be confined to the disputes referred, the parties to those disputes, and those who agreed to refer them. The union failed to produce evidence that the resolution amendments were sent to or registered by the Registrar as required by sections 6(g), 28(3), 29, and 30(3) of the Trade Unions Act and regulation 9 of the Central Trade Union Regulations; hence, extending the award to other establishments was without jurisdiction. Under service conditions, total hours were 39 hours per week. While the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act fixes maximum hours at 48 hours a week and double wages beyond that, paying ordinary wages for work between 39 and 48 hours would provide no extra compensation and would indirectly alter conditions of service; thus, the Tribunal did not err in fixing the overtime rate. Regarding special leave, the company already allowed union representatives paid leave for conciliation and tribunal proceedings. The Tribunal failed to consider the adverse impact of further absenteeism on production, and could not limit the indefinite number of meetings or delegates. Executive committee meetings could be held outside work hours or covered by earned leave during emergencies, as could federation meetings and INTUC conventions.
sections.judgement: The Supreme Court held that: (i) The award was operative only in respect of the workmen of the appellant company's factory at Jamshedpur and not the workmen of its other establishments; (ii) The overtime rate fixed by the Tribunal was confirmed as the Tribunal did not err or act unjustly; and (iii) The demand for special leave was disallowed.

sections.facts: The appellant applied for a contract carriage permit valid throughout the State of Karnataka, proposing to use his vehicle in all nineteen regions, to the Regional Transport Authority, Mandya. The Authority granted the permit on February 8, 1972, on the basis that the Mandya region had more motorable roads than any other district in the State. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal cancelled the permit by order dated August 19, 1972, on an appeal by the State Road Transport Corporation. The appellant's writ petition before the Karnataka High Court challenging this cancellation was dismissed, leading to an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court.
sections.statute: Section 45(1) of the Act is a general provision regulating applications for inter-regional route permits within a State, requiring an application to be made to the appropriate Regional Transport Authority mentioned in the proviso: either to the Regional Transport Authority of the region in which the major portion of the proposed route or area lies, or to the Regional Transport Authority of the region in which it is proposed to keep the vehicle(s) if the portions in each region are approximately equal. Section 2(1) defines 'area' as an area specifically notified by the State Government, and 'route' is defined in the Act as a line of travel specifying the highway which may be traversed by a motor vehicle between one terminus and another.
sections.argument: The State Road Transport Corporation contended that geographically the Mandya region was smaller in area and, as such, the jurisdiction of the Regional Transport Authority, Mandya was ousted. Additionally, questions were raised regarding the reasonableness of requiring an application for an inter-regional permit to be made to the Regional Transport Authority of the region where the major portion of the proposed route or area lies.
sections.analysis: The terms and expressions defined in Section 2 apply only if there is nothing repugnant in the subject or context. Because the first proviso to Section 45(1) speaks of the route or area proposed in an application for a permit, there is no question of the State Government specifying the area; thus, the definition of 'area' in Section 2(1) has no relevance in this context. While a route is defined as a line of travel between two termini on a highway, the idea of a route as a notional line has not been consistently maintained in the Act. A route can mean both the notional line of travel and the area of the route over which motor vehicles ply, yet 'route' and 'area' are not interchangeable—a route is an area plus the notional line of travel between two termini. A contract carriage does not ply along a fixed route but over an area. Therefore, the word 'area' in the first proviso to Section 45(1) means the area of motorable roads within the territorial jurisdiction of a regional transport authority, as geographical area district-wise is irrelevant to the purpose of the Act. Jurisdiction to grant an inter-regional permit depends on the existing areas of motorable roads at the time the application is made. Furthermore, the Court observed that the reasonableness of the provision is a matter of policy that has not been stated very clearly, suggesting that the State should clarify the law by appropriate legislation instead of leaving it in a slippery state.

sections.facts: An agreement was entered into by appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and respondent No. 1 regarding partition of joint movable and immovable properties. A dispute arose relating to certain properties, which was referred to arbitration. The arbitrators made their award on November 28, 1977, which was filed by them before the Sub Judge on January 28, 1978, pursuant to an application made by appellants Nos. 1 to 4 under section 14 of the Arbitration Act. On December 1, 1977, respondent No. 1 had filed an application under section 11 of the Arbitration Act before the Munsif, who passed an injunction order on July 26, 1978, for maintaining status quo till the disposal of the said application. On an application made by the arbitrators on August 14, 1978, the Sub Judge ordered on September 2, 1978, the return of the award to the arbitrators to enable them to present it for registration before the Sub Registrar. The High Court in appeal set aside this order, holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction to maintain status quo, the arbitrators could not take back the award for registration, and ordered that the application be kept pending until the injunction was vacated. On December 20, 1982, the Munsif dismissed the case of respondent No. 1 and the interim injunction was ipso facto discharged. Thereafter, the Subordinate Judge dismissed the arbitrators' application for return of the award, holding that the limitation for registration had expired. The High Court, in appeal, directed the Subordinate Judge to return the award, holding that it was the Registrar and not the Sub Judge who could determine limitation for registration. On November 24, 1983, the arbitrators got back the award and presented it the next day before the Sub Registrar, who registered it the same day. On a petition by respondent No. 1 challenging the registration, the High Court remitted the award to the Sub Registrar to reconsider the limitation issue. The Sub Registrar found the presentation was within time because the pendency of judicial proceedings from January 28, 1978 to November 24, 1983 was to be excluded under section 15 of the Limitation Act. On a subsequent application by respondent No. 1, the High Court quashed the registration, holding that the award was presented beyond time. The validity and propriety of that order was challenged in appeal by special leave.
sections.statute: Sections 23 and 25 of the Registration Act; Section 14 and Section 11 of the Arbitration Act; Section 15 of the Limitation Act.
sections.analysis: Under the Registration Act, the limitation period for registration is four months from the date of execution, and where the delay in presentation does not exceed four months, the document may be accepted for registration on payment of a fine. The cumulative effect of sections 23 and 25 read together is that a total period of eight months is available for registration if the requisite conditions are fulfilled. In the instant case, the award was made on November 28, 1977, and before the expiry of four months, it was filed in court pursuant to an order of the court. From July 26, 1978 to December 20, 1982, a subsisting injunction prevented the arbitrators from taking any steps. Furthermore, as the award remained in the custody of the court from January 28, 1978 until its return on November 24, 1983, neither the arbitrators nor the parties could have presented it for registration during that time. The award was presented before the Sub Registrar on November 25, 1983, the very next day after getting possession from the court. The period during which judicial proceedings were pending from January 28, 1978 to November 24, 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle in section 15 of the Limitation Act. The High Court was wrong in excluding only the period of the interim injunction (July 26, 1978 till December 20, 1982), because the award remained in the custody of the court and the court had declined the arbitrators' attempts to obtain it. The legal maxims 'lex non cogit ad impossibilia' (the law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform) and 'actus curiae neminem gravabit' (an act of the court shall prejudice no man) apply with full vigour to the facts.
sections.judgement: Appeal by special leave allowed.

sections.facts: The respondent had let out his house to a firm against whom he obtained permission from the Rent Control Authority to terminate the tenancy on the ground of arrears of rent. Meanwhile, the tenant intimated to the respondent by telegram that he had vacated the premises, but prior to the receipt of the telegram, the appellant had applied to the Additional Deputy Commissioner that since the premises were likely to fall vacant, they should be allotted to him as he was a displaced person, and provisional allotment was made in his favour and he continued to be in possession since then. The respondent then moved for the cancellation of the said allotment on the ground that he needed the premises for his own use, but the allotment was confirmed in favour of the appellant by the Additional Deputy Commissioner. The respondent then filed a writ petition in the High Court for cancellation of the said order, which was set aside and the case was remanded for disposal in accordance with law; against this the appellant filed a Letters Patent Appeal. On remand the earlier order was confirmed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, against which the respondent filed another writ petition in the High Court. The Letters Patent Appeal and the subsequent writ petition were heard together and the High Court allowed the writ petition and set aside the order of allotment in favour of the appellant on the ground that as soon as it appeared that the appellant had a place of business of his own, he ceased to be a displaced person within the meaning of cl. 23(1) and the other relevant clauses.
sections.analysis: Clause 23(1) refers to the persons in the specified categories and empowers the Deputy Commissioner to make an order of allotment in their favour. There are no terms of limitation qualifying the said persons and the scheme of the relevant provision does not seem to contemplate any such limitation. Clause 23(1), as well as cls. 24 and 24A do not necessarily exclude the cases of persons specified in them on the ground that the said persons already have an accommodation of their own.
sections.judgement: The High Court was in error in assuming that the provisions of cls. 23(1), 24 and 24A impliedly postulated that the persons belonging to the respective categories specified by them could receive allotment only if they had no previous accommodation of their own. Further, after remand the Additional Deputy Commissioner did not properly appreciate the scope and effect of the provision contained in the relevant clause and he took an unduly narrow view of the limits of the enquiry which he was bound to hold as a result of the remand order and that has vitiated his final conclusion.
